---

Understanding the role of motivation in student engagement with laboratory skill education is essential for promoting learning and academic achievement. Physical laboratories in science education are widely regarded as experiential learning environments that support the development of higher-order conceptual understanding. Students’ attitudes toward these laboratories significantly influence the effectiveness of skill training. During the COVID-19 pandemic, computer-based virtual laboratories (VLs) emerged as a promising alternative for laboratory instruction and experimentation, particularly under lockdown conditions. However, the adoption of VLs remains limited, largely due to insufficient awareness of, and familiarity with, these tools among teachers and students.

This study examined the key motivational factors influencing the effectiveness of VLs in teaching laboratory skills and tasks to students. Data were collected through a survey-based approach using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI), self-reported measures of extrinsic factors, and a teachers’ perception scale regarding VLs. The data were analyzed using independent-samples t-tests and automatic linear modeling (LINEAR). The findings indicate that animated graphic learning materials in VLs had a stronger positive effect on students’ intrinsic motivation than e-book-based materials. Teachers also played a critical role in enhancing students’ motivation to conduct laboratory experiments through VLs. In addition, the results suggest that repeated or prolonged engagement with VL experiments positively influenced students’ laboratory performance.

---
